ext.title: Empirical Models of Lobbying
ext.venue: Annual Review of Economics 12:391-413 (first published online May 13, 2020)
ext.document_type: Review article (narrative literature review; no original estimation or sample). Metadata hint verified against the PDF front matter; no correction needed.
ext.coverage: Full text read in full (text file lines 1-1170, covering journal pp. 391-413 including the literature cited list). Annotation file read in full: 106 highlights, zero sticky notes, so no note text exists. Page numbers in the annotation file are PDF page indices (PDF page n corresponds to journal page n+390).
ext.research_question: Is lobbying (direct or intermediated business-government interaction over policy) welfare-enhancing or welfare-distorting? The review organizes recent empirical work on quid pro quo and informational lobbying, asks how to identify policy supply and demand and the counterfactual equilibrium with no lobbying, and assesses how distorted equilibrium policy is relative to the social optimum.
ext.theory: Quid pro quo perspective: Grossman and Helpman (1994, 1996) menu-auction and electoral models; policy supply and demand framework (lD = C Q^(1-1/eps), lS = G Q^(1+1/eta)), Figure 1; Tullock (1967) contest function as used by Kang (2016); bargaining across heterogeneous special interests (Bombardini and Trebbi 2011). Informational perspective: cheap talk (Crawford and Sobel 1982; Krishna and Morgan 2001; Battaglini 2002), costly or money-burning signaling (Potters and van Winden 1992; Grossman and Helpman 2001), hybrid access-fee models (Austen-Smith 1995; Lohmann 1995), legislative subsidy (Hall and Deardorff 2006), and information verification by lobbying intermediaries (Groll and Ellis 2014; Hirsch et al. 2019).
ext.data: No original data. Sources surveyed: LDA filings via Senate Office of Public Records (SOPR) and CRP (total lobbying about $3-3.5 billion per year over the decade to 2019 versus $200-250 million PAC donations; average 12,537 unique lobbyists per year 1998-2019, 11,654 in 2018; about 37,000 active lobbyists 1999-2008 per Bertrand et al. 2014); FEC and CRP PAC data; LobbyView/Compustat (Huneeus and Kim 2019: 766 of 7,646 US public firms lobbied in 2017); Washington Representatives directory (about 14,000 of 37,000 lobbyists profiled); LegiStorm staffer salaries (2012); Kang (2016) 538 energy policies in 445 bills, 110th Congress; Hirsch et al. (2019) 219 FARA lobbyists, 110th-111th Congress; federal rulemaking comments from 150 agencies (Bertrand et al. 2018a); Canada Registry (about 9,000 lobbyists, 2017-18); EU Transparency Register (5,431 registrants in 2012, 11,901 in 2018).
ext.method: Narrative review organized as quid pro quo (structural econometric and reduced-form) versus informational. Structural methods reviewed: Kang (2016) Tullock-contest game with simulated maximum likelihood and equilibrium selection; Bombardini and Trebbi (2011) structural first-order conditions yielding a dollar-per-vote cost; Huneeus and Kim (2019) heterogeneous-firm general-equilibrium model estimated by minimum distance on simulated moments. Reduced-form methods reviewed: difference-in-differences (Blanes i Vidal et al. 2012), instrumental variables (de Figueiredo and Silverman 2006 with overhead rates; Goldstein and You 2017 with distance to Washington), natural experiments (Kerr et al. 2014 H-1B cap; Dellavigna et al. 2016 Berlusconi advertising), and observational contact and mobility regressions (Bertrand et al. 2014; Hirsch et al. 2019). Text methods: NLP to classify bill policies (Kang 2016, p.397) and latent semantic analysis of comments (Bertrand et al. 2018a, p.408, n.35).
ext.identification: Varies by paper. Huneeus and Kim (2019): committee-assignment shocks to senators connected to firms (p.401, n.18). Kang (2016): equilibrium selection (maximizes sum of payoffs) and simulated counterfactual with no lobbying. de Figueiredo and Silverman (2006): university overhead rates shift policy demand (p.403). Goldstein and You (2017): political mismatch between city and state, with distance from Washington as IV (p.403, n.20). Kerr et al. (2014): predetermined H-1B cap expiry, differential exposure (p.404). Blanes i Vidal et al. (2012): exit of connected senator, assumed exogenous (p.404). Dellavigna et al. (2016): Berlusconi office-holding shifts ad spending to Mediaset (p.405-406). Bertrand et al. (2014): committee reassignment of politicians and lobbyist following (p.405).
ext.scope: Population: mainly US federal lobbying (LDA data 1999-2019 with 1998 onward totals), public and business interests, mostly the Congress and federal agencies; secondary sections on Canada (Sec. 5.1) and EU (Sec. 5.2). Institutions: Congress, federal agencies, Senate and House committees, and EU Commission and Parliament. Era: literature from the 1990s through 2019, with some references to 1971 FECA disclosure rules and the 2007 LDA amendments.

key_findings.finding: Survey context: 53% of respondents called lobbyists and special interest groups in Washington a very big problem, versus 38% for illegal immigration (Pew surveys, Sept 2018-Mar 2019).
Kang (2016) energy-sector lobbying: only 8% of 538 policies in 445 bills are enacted; policies with no lobbying are enacted about 1% of the time; policies with two or more lobbying players about 24%.
key_findings.numbers: 8% overall; 1% no lobbying; 24% two or more lobbyists

key_findings.finding: Kang's model implies lobbying raises enactment by only 0.021% to 0.415% over an 8% baseline, and average returns to lobbying of 137% (renewables) to 152% (oil and gas). The implied monetary value per policy above $500 million is flagged by the authors as possibly signaling misspecification.

Bombardini and Trebbi (2011) structural bargaining model on Congressional campaign contributions estimates $200-$400 of donations per vote acquired and a precise average rate of return on political spending. Adding the electoral-vote channel makes implied returns far more reasonable.
key_findings.numbers: $200-$400 per vote; agriculture return about $13.7 per dollar at the margin; simulated returns 10%-20% per year

key_findings.finding: Farm Bill comparison: about $22 billion in 2000 agribusiness subsidies against under $3.7 million in agribusiness PAC contributions implies a naive return of about 600,000%, which the authors argue shows that observable contributions miss other influence channels.

Huneeus and Kim (2019): a 10% increase in lobbying raises revenue 3%. Federal lobbying reduces aggregate US productivity 22%, with 59% from misallocation to lobbying (less productive) firms and 41% from missing entry of productive firms.

Huneeus and Kim lobbying facts: 766 of 7,646 US public firms lobbied in 2017; lobbying firms have about four times the revenue of non-lobbying firms; elasticity of lobbying to sales about one conditional on lobbying.
Lobbying is persistent: 92% of firms that lobby in a year also lobby the next year (Kerr et al. 2014), consistent with large sunk entry costs.

Industry-association share: individual firms account for an average 67% (median 96%) of lobbying per Bombardini and Trebbi (2012), and industries with lower concentration and differentiation use trade associations more.

Scale of federal lobbying: total spending about $3-3.5 billion per year over the decade, versus $200-250 million per year in PAC donations; about 12,537 unique lobbyists per year 1998-2019 on average.

Earmarks (de Figueiredo and Silverman 2006): an extra dollar of lobbying yields about one dollar more in earmarks for universities with no Appropriations-committee ties, and $4.52-$5.24 for universities with connections.
Goldstein and You (2017) cities: approximate return of $1.02 in earmarks and $0.47 in 2009 Recovery Act grants per $1 of lobbying, using distance-based IV.

Kerr et al. (2014): after the H-1B visa cap reduction, high-skill-immigration lobbying as a share of total lobbying doubles for dependent firms; the effect is stronger for firms that lobbied on other issues before, consistent with fixed entry costs.

Blanes i Vidal et al. (2012): revolving-door lobbyists (former aides) lose a persistent 24% of lobbying revenue when their connected senator exits office. Drops are larger for Finance, Appropriations, or Ways and Means connections and insignificant otherwise; the exit-exogeneity assumption is flagged as strong.

Bertrand et al. (2014): about 37,000 active lobbyists in 1999-2008; in-house share fell from nearly 60% to under 40%; external lobbying doubled 1999-2008. Lobbyists follow politicians across committees, and the expertise premium does not rise with issue relevance, which the authors read as access dominating expertise.
key_findings.numbers: about 37,000 lobbyists; in-house share 60% to <40%; external lobbying doubled

key_findings.finding: Dellavigna et al. (2016): regulated firms in Italy shift advertising onto Berlusconi-owned Mediaset during his periods in office, only in heavily regulated industries, at a scale of hundreds of millions of euros.

Hirsch et al. (2019) FARA data: lobbying contact is more likely with ideologically aligned Members, and conditional on contact, lobbyists with ideological closeness or prior connections bring fewer clients and set higher certification thresholds.
Bertrand et al. (2018a) with latent semantic analysis of rulemaking comments from 150 agencies: a nonprofit comment's similarity to its benefactor's comments rises immediately after a donation.

Canada: about 9,000 registered lobbyists in 2017-18, just over 1,000 external; compared with 11,654 US lobbyists in the same year. Hickey (2014) finds only 6% of Canadian lobbyists follow reshuffled ministers.

EU: the voluntary Transparency Register grew from 5,431 registrants (2012) to 11,901 (2018). Apple reported EUR 2-2.25 million of EU lobbying in 2018 versus $6.7 million in the US. Dellis and Sondermann (2017) match about 2,000 Orbis firms to the register.

limitations: Authors state that the two main unresolved issues are how to account for lobbying's effect on which equilibrium policies are chosen, and how distorted those policies are relative to the social optimum (abstract, p.391); a comprehensive welfare assessment is described as elusive.
Authors caution that the review resolves little of the good-or-bad question (Sec. 1, p.392).
Lobbying may be invisible to researchers when it blocks change, leaving only a status quo with no visible law change (p.393).

Informational models are rare in empirical work because data on the informational needs of agents and on transmitted expertise are very hard to obtain (p.394). Information is hard to quantify (p.393).

Structural models show signs of misspecification: Kang's near-zero lobbying effect and $500m+ implied value per policy (pp.398-399); the authors say some structural models display symptoms of misspecification (p.410).
Structural identification is not assured: Huneeus and Kim's minimum-distance criterion may not have a unique minimizer and should be probed with Monte Carlo (p.401).
Kang (2016) equilibrium multiplicity: equilibrium is selected by maximizing total payoffs; budget constraints are excluded and games treated as independent (p.398, n.14).

Exogeneity and exclusion assumptions: Blanes i Vidal et al. assume senator exit is orthogonal to lobbyist fortunes, which is strong if senators retire strategically (p.404); distance IV in Goldstein and You is open to exclusion-restriction criticism (p.403, n.20); Goldstein and You do not use cumulative transfers (p.403, n.21).

Measurement of lobbying effects: Kang's policy-level and bill-level mapping needed heavy preprocessing; omitting bill refinement would mismeasure lobbying effects (p.398, n.12). Lobbying spending alone is not the full influence arsenal (Sec. 2, p.394).

Cross-country comparability limited: Canadian Registry lacks fee data (p.409); EU register is voluntary with limited history, and EU firm counts are not directly comparable with Compustat counts (p.410).

rel.summary_md:
Bombardini and Trebbi (2020) is a narrative review of empirical lobbying research. It contains no new estimation. It sorts the literature into quid pro quo models, where political resources are exchanged for policy, and informational models, where interest groups pass expertise to less-informed policymakers. It then asks how each line of work identifies policy supply and demand and the counterfactual of no lobbying.

The review reaches three conclusions that matter for Paul's systems.

First, structural estimates of what money buys are fragile. Kang (2016) estimates that lobbying raises enactment by only 0.021% to 0.415% over an 8% baseline (538 energy policies, 110th Congress), yet the same model implies more than $500m of value per policy. A naive Farm Bill comparison gives a return near 600,000% ($22bn of 2000 subsidies against under $3.7m of agribusiness PAC money). The authors read these figures as symptoms of misspecification or of influence channels left out of the model. Adding an electoral-vote channel (Bombardini and Trebbi 2011) brings implied returns down to plausible levels.

Second, lobbying is persistent: 92% of firms that lobby in one year lobby the next (Kerr et al. 2014). The structure of the industry has also shifted: from 1999 to 2008 the in-house share of lobbying fell from about 60% to under 40%, while external lobbying doubled.

Third, in the revolving-door literature, a lobbyist's revenue depends on the patron staying in office. Former aides lose a persistent 24% of revenue when their senator exits (Blanes i Vidal et al. 2012), and lobbyists follow politicians across committee reassignments (Bertrand et al. 2014).

For the system as built, the review supports keeping money a minority, saturating channel in the flip and money-response engines, and treating ROI figures as fragile. It supports the persistence-based lobbying nowcast in Mentat and the rule that in-house and outside-firm lobbying are never summed. It also exposes one gap: the staffer route costs decay with time since overlap but do not account for whether the anchoring member is still in office or holds a powerful committee seat.

bearings.paper_claim: Kang (2016) structural Tullock-contest model: lobbying raises enactment probability by only 0.021%-0.415% over an 8% baseline (538 policies in 445 bills, 110th Congress), while implied returns are 137%-152%. Large observed stakes paired with small contributions point to influence channels that observable money does not capture.
bearings.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b), where money is the minority partner (WM 0.35 vs peer weight WP 0.65). The money term saturates relative to the member's receipts (HALFF 0.10), on the stated premise that money buys access and effort more than votes.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Kang measures firm lobbying expenditure against bill-level enactment in the energy sector. Melange's money leg is PAC contributions against member-level winnability on CU topics. The review supports only the direction (small marginal effect of money), not the WM/WP split or the HALFF constant, which remain unestimated design choices. The evidence is federal and from 2007-08.

bearings.paper_claim: Observed money-to-outcome ratios imply implausible returns: Kang's model implies more than $500m of value per policy, and the Farm Bill comparison gives a naive return of about 600,000% ($22bn in 2000 subsidies vs under $3.7m in agribusiness PAC money). The authors treat 'excessive returns' as common in this literature and as a sign of misspecification. Returns become reasonable only once an electoral-vote channel is modeled (Bombardini and Trebbi 2011: $200-$400 per vote; 10%-20% simulated annual return).
bearings.system_side: Closed-form break-even CU spend against competitor money, using the same saturating share-type money term, plus member ROI floor values checked by roi_verify.py.
bearings.code_ref: fec/engine/money_response.py:68-75 (shared saturating money form); fec/templates/make_dashboard_html_00.tpl (break-even, path only)
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a caution about any ROI read off contribution-to-outcome ratios. It applies directly whenever dashboard ROI floors are presented as returns. It does not invalidate the break-even algebra, which is internal to the model. Any ROI shown should carry an UNVERIFIED or model-output label.

bearings.paper_claim: Structural and reduced-form work finds small marginal policy effects of money, despite large stakes (Kang 0.021%-0.415% enactment lift). Contributions are low, and caps rarely bind.
bearings.system_side: MAXSHIFT was cut from 40 to 18 on the premise that money moves positions little. A defection requires a donation of about one sixth of the member's receipts, so a $10k gift shifts median receipts by about 0.9 lean, far below DTHRESH 11.25.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The review addresses enactment and bill outcomes, not shifts in individual member stance. It supports rare money-triggered defection but not the LOSSFRAME 1.10 asymmetry or the specific constants.

bearings.paper_claim: Lobbying is highly persistent: 92% of firms that lobby in one year also lobby the next (Kerr et al. 2014), consistent with large sunk entry costs. Lobbying expenditure has an elasticity of about 1 to sales, conditional on lobbying (Huneeus and Kim 2019).
bearings.system_side: The lobbying projection is an in-year nowcast (amount filed so far plus (1-s) times the prior full year), carried forward unchanged. Its bands come from LobbyView persistence error. The earlier year-effect slope model never beat last-period naive (G9).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The 92% figure is a firm-level extensive-margin rate (does a firm lobby at all), not dollar-level persistence for an industry. Sector aggregation should make levels smoother still, which favors persistence. The review offers no evidence on how lobbying dollars move within a cycle.

bearings.paper_claim: The composition of lobbying shifted: from 1999 to 2008 the in-house share fell from nearly 60% to under 40%, and external lobbying doubled (Bertrand et al. 2014; about 37,000 active lobbyists over 1999-2008).
bearings.system_side: The lobbying card shows hired-firm income and in-house expenses side by side and never adds them. The sector-growth config also records that the undifferentiated LobbyView sum double-counts self-filers' outside-firm fees (a median of 9-26%).
bearings.transfer_conditions: These are shares of all federal LDA lobbying over 1999-2008. Composition by finance or CU sector is not reported, so this supports showing the two channels separately but provides no sector-specific shares.

bearings.paper_claim: Individual firms account for a mean of 67% (median 96%) of their industry's lobbying (Bombardini and Trebbi 2012). Industries with lower concentration and less product differentiation lean more on trade associations.
bearings.system_side: Finance clients are classified bank, CU or other from client names. The brain records that directional positions sit with trade associations (CUNA 174 Support / 12 Oppose, NAFCU 168 Support / 23 Oppose; pinned fintech and crypto firms hold 1 directional position out of 56). ABA lobbying is $228M against CUNA's $93M.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The prediction is cross-industry, from Bombardini and Trebbi's 2012 sample. Credit unions are an extreme low-concentration industry, so trade-association dominance is the expected pattern. The review gives no CU-specific figure.

bearings.paper_claim: Revolving-door lobbyists who are former aides lose a persistent 24% of lobbying revenue when their connected senator exits office (Blanes i Vidal et al. 2012). The drop is larger for Finance, Appropriations and Ways and Means connections and insignificant otherwise. Lobbyists also follow their politicians across committee reassignments (Bertrand et al. 2014).
bearings.system_side: Route cost uses time-decayed exposure (5-year staleness half-life), workplace concentration and a member-context modifier built from cosponsor-graph proximity times eigenvector centrality. None of these reads whether the anchoring member is still serving or which committee the member sits on.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The evidence measures lobbyists' revenue and covers senators' staff from 1998 to 2008. It is not a measure of introduction success, closeness or influence. Under the brain's D-025 rule and the revolving-door wording rule, an added term may be described only as dependence on the patron's current office. It must not be labelled access or influence. Blanes i Vidal's exogeneity assumption on senator exit is flagged as strong.

bearings.paper_claim: Kang (2016) models lobbying as Tullock contests between opposing special-interest coalitions, mapped at the level of policy provisions inside bills. Policies with no lobbying are enacted about 1% of the time and policies with two or more lobbying players about 24% (descriptive). The structural effect of lobbying is much smaller (0.021%-0.415%).
bearings.system_side: A per-bill contested or advisory registry with explicit counterparty industries. The loader has shipped. No engine consumer exists, and the CONTESTED_V1 dial is only planned.
bearings.transfer_conditions: A contest success function is the natural form for the planned counterparty term, but Kang's own model carries known misspecification symptoms and selects among multiple equilibria by assumption. The 1% vs 24% contrast reflects selection and must not be quoted as a lobbying effect. Weighting contests by LDA spend would conflict with D-021.

bearings.paper_claim: Informational and legislative-subsidy accounts (Hall and Deardorff 2006) and FARA evidence (Hirsch et al. 2019; 219 lobbyists, 110th-111th Congress) show that lobbying contact is more likely with ideologically aligned members. Lobbying works by subsidising allies rather than converting opponents.
bearings.system_side: Members whose overall tier is Skeptic, Highly Skeptical or Opponent receive zero money in every allocator. The gate fails open for members with no matrix row.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The evidence concerns lobbyist contact under FARA (foreign principals), not domestic PAC dollars. It is consistent with funding allies but does not test whether contributions to opposed members change their positions.

bearings.paper_claim: Huneeus and Kim (2019; LobbyView and Compustat): 766 of 7,646 public firms lobbied in 2017. Lobbying firms have about 4x the revenue of non-lobbying firms. The elasticity of lobbying to sales is about 1, conditional on lobbying. A 10% increase in lobbying raises revenue by 3%. Identification comes from committee-assignment shocks.
bearings.system_side: Sector-year regressions of log giving and log lobbying on lagged sector growth, with year-FE variants. The lobbying lead flips sign under year FE, and growth adds no adjusted R2.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The review's figures are firm-level, cross-sectional size elasticities in a single year. They do not predict a within-sector growth-to-spending effect once year shocks are absorbed, so the study's null result does not conflict with them. The figures should not be cited as support for the deep-pockets hypothesis at sector-year grain.

gaps_exposed: Staffer and revolving-door routing has no term for whether the anchoring member is still in office or sits on a high-stakes committee (Finance, Appropriations, Ways and Means). The review's strongest revolving-door evidence ties a connection's revenue value to exactly those facts, while the system models only time decay since overlap.

There is no independent contact measure for lobbying. LD-2 filings never name members, and the review's contact-level evidence comes from FARA (Hirsch et al.), whose coverage excludes the domestic CU and bank clients this system tracks.

The planned contested-bill counterparty term has no functional form. The review's main structural template (a Tullock contest between opposing coalitions) relies on equilibrium selection and shows misspecification symptoms.

The system has no informational channel. Every money and lobbying lever is quid pro quo or pressure, while the review treats the informational view (cheap talk, legislative subsidy, opposing-bias senders) as one of the two main families.
No owner-ratified mechanism checks ROI and break-even outputs for plausibility. The review shows returns computed from observable contributions are routinely implausible.
flags: D-104..D-108: the review does not validate the competitiveness reciprocity premise. Bombardini and Trebbi (2011) has an electoral-vote channel via persuadable voters, but it does not estimate that dollars buy more in competitive seats. Do not cite this paper for COMPET_MULT.

Revolving-door wording rule: Blanes i Vidal's 24% figure is a revenue loss for former aides turned lobbyists. Any use in staffer routing must avoid influence or access language, and under D-025 it must not be treated as an introduction probability.
D-021: a Kang-style contest weighted by LDA spend would use LDA as a weight source. A contested-bills extension built that way needs an owner ruling first.

Kang's descriptive enactment rates (1% with no lobbying vs 24% with two or more lobbying players) carry selection bias and are not a lobbying effect. The review's own structural estimate is 0.021%-0.415%.
The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). Nothing to flag on those.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul recorded no takeaway for this paper; both annotation entries are empty. Measured against his positions on other components, the review backs the system's conservative stance over his ROI enthusiasm. It shows that contribution-based returns are routinely implausible, which is consistent with his calling the Alexander figure an outlier, and it supports keeping money a minority channel in the flip model. It also reports the Huneeus and Kim committee-assignment instrument he cites for the committee pillar. The review does not mention competitive-seat effects, so it gives no support to his Cook PVI responsiveness reading. His notes predate the persistence-based lobbying nowcast and the never-summed in-house/outside rule. The review supports both, so nothing in his notes needs revising on those points.

related.why: The review summarises Huneeus and Kim's GE model: a 22% productivity loss, a 59/41 misallocation-versus-entry split, and the committee-assignment identification, along with a warning that the minimum-distance minimiser may not be unique.
LobbyView is the firm-level data source behind the reviewed counts (766 of 7,646 public firms lobbying in 2017).
The review's warning that observed lobbying returns are implausibly large applies to Alexander's ROI estimate, which Paul already treats as an outlier.
Both separate lobbying from PAC money. The review puts lobbying at $3-3.5bn a year against $200-250m in PAC donations, and Furnas et al. show low organisational overlap between the two.
The review's account of money as access with a small policy effect matches Kalla and Broockman's field evidence that contributions buy access.
Kang's mapping of policies to bills, which the review describes as needing heavy preprocessing, is the problem that LLM-based position extraction from lobbying reports addresses.
The review's access-versus-expertise result (Bertrand et al.) bears on Holyoke's question of which lobbying skills can be taught.
DIME ideology scores are one of the measures the review reports for Hirsch et al.'s contact analysis.
DW-NOMINATE is the ideology measure in the reviewed FARA contact study.
Both treat donations and lobbying as linked instruments. The review stresses substitution across influence tools, citing Bombardini and Trebbi (2011).
Both relate firm lobbying and PAC activity to firm size and concentration, the facts the review reports from Huneeus and Kim.
Partisan ties of lobbying firms extend the review's evidence that lobbyists' value rests on connections to particular politicians.
